notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Electricity deals with electric charges, their motion and their effects.
  • Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter.
  • There are two types of electric charge: positive and negative.
  • Like charges repel each other.
  • Unlike charges attract each other.
  • Electric current is the directed flow of electric charge.
  • The SI unit of electric charge is coulomb.
  • The SI unit of electric current is ampere.
  • The SI unit of potential difference is volt.
  • The SI unit of resistance is ohm.
  • Electricity may be classified broadly as static electricity and current electricity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Charge → Coulomb

Current → Ampere

Potential Difference → Volt

Resistance → Ohm

2. Electric Charge
  • Electric charge is represented by Q or q.
  • The SI unit of charge is coulomb.
  • The symbol for coulomb is C.
  • Positive charge is associated with deficiency of electrons in ordinary charging processes.
  • Negative charge is associated with excess electrons.
  • Charge is a scalar quantity.
  • Electric charge is quantised.
  • Electric charge is conserved.
3. Elementary Charge
  • The magnitude of charge on one proton is approximately +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • The magnitude of charge on one electron is approximately −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • The magnitude of elementary charge is represented by e.
  • e ≈ 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • One coulomb corresponds to approximately 6.24 × 10¹⁸ elementary charges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electron charge → −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

Proton charge → +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

4. Quantisation of Charge
  • Electric charge occurs in integral multiples of the elementary charge.
  • Q = ne.
  • n is an integer.
  • e is elementary charge.
  • The concept of elementary charge is important in atomic physics.
5. Conservation of Charge
  • Total electric charge of an isolated system remains constant.
  • Charge can be transferred from one body to another.
  • Charge is not created or destroyed in ordinary processes.
  • When one body gains electrons, another may lose an equal amount of negative charge.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Charge → Conserved

6. Static Electricity
  • Static electricity refers to electric charges accumulated on objects.
  • Static charges are commonly produced through friction, contact or induction.
  • Rubbing certain materials transfers electrons between surfaces.
  • Static charge can produce attraction or repulsion.
  • A sudden discharge of static charge can produce a spark.
  • Lightning is a large-scale electrostatic discharge.
7. Charging by Friction
  • Friction can transfer electrons between materials.
  • Protons normally remain bound within atomic nuclei.
  • A body gaining electrons becomes negatively charged.
  • A body losing electrons becomes positively charged.
  • Rubbing a glass rod with silk is a traditional electrostatic example.
  • Rubbing an ebonite rod with fur is another traditional example.
8. Charging by Conduction
  • Charging by conduction requires physical contact.
  • A charged body touches another conducting body.
  • Electrons redistribute between them.
  • The second body may acquire charge of the same sign as the charging body under common arrangements.
9. Charging by Induction
  • Charging by induction can occur without direct contact.
  • A nearby charged object causes redistribution of charges in a conductor.
  • Grounding may be used to leave the conductor with a net charge.
  • The induced final charge can be opposite to that of the inducing body.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Conduction → Contact

Induction → No direct contact required

10. Conductors
  • Conductors allow electric charge to move relatively easily.
  • Metals are good electrical conductors.
  • Copper is widely used for electrical wiring.
  • Aluminium is also used as an electrical conductor.
  • Silver has very high electrical conductivity.
  • Human body conducts electricity because it contains water and dissolved ions.
  • Graphite conducts electricity despite being a non-metal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Common wiring metal → Copper

Non-metal conductor → Graphite

11. Insulators
  • Insulators strongly resist movement of electric charge.
  • Rubber is an electrical insulator.
  • Plastic is an insulator.
  • Glass is an insulator.
  • Dry wood is a relatively poor conductor.
  • Ceramic materials are used as insulators in electrical systems.
  • Insulation prevents accidental contact with live conductors.
12. Semiconductor
  • A semiconductor has electrical conductivity between that of conductors and insulators.
  • Silicon is a widely used semiconductor.
  • Germanium is also a semiconductor.
  • Semiconductor conductivity can be controlled by doping.
  • Diodes and transistors are made using semiconductors.
  • Semiconductor devices are central to modern electronics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Silicon → Semiconductor

13. Electric Current
  • Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
  • Current is represented by I.
  • I = Q/t.
  • Q is charge.
  • t is time.
  • SI unit is ampere.
  • One ampere equals one coulomb per second.
  • 1 A = 1 C/s.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Current → I = Q/t

14. Ampere
  • Ampere is the SI unit of electric current.
  • The symbol is A.
  • The unit is named after André-Marie Ampère.
  • 1 ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point per second.
15. Conventional Current
  • Conventional current is defined as the direction in which positive charge would flow.
  • In metallic conductors, electrons move opposite to conventional current.
  • Conventional current flows from higher electric potential to lower potential through the external circuit.
  • Electron flow in metals is from negative terminal toward positive terminal through the external circuit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Conventional current direction → Opposite to electron drift in metal wires.

16. Drift of Electrons
  • Free electrons in a conductor move randomly because of thermal motion.
  • When an electric field is applied, electrons acquire a small net drift velocity.
  • This directed drift produces electric current.
  • Electron drift velocity is much smaller than the speed at which an electrical signal propagates through a circuit.
17. Electric Potential
  • Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge.
  • SI unit of electric potential is volt.
  • Electric potential is a scalar quantity.
  • Potential can be positive, negative or zero relative to a chosen reference.
18. Potential Difference
  • Potential difference is work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points.
  • V = W/Q.
  • V is potential difference.
  • W is work or energy.
  • Q is charge.
  • SI unit is volt.
  • One volt equals one joule per coulomb.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 V = 1 J/C

19. Voltage
  • Voltage is another term commonly used for electric potential difference.
  • Voltage provides the driving influence that can produce current in a circuit.
  • A battery maintains potential difference between its terminals.
  • Voltage does not itself mean current is flowing if the circuit is open.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Potential difference can exist even when current is zero.

20. Resistance
  • Resistance is opposition to electric current.
  • Resistance is represented by R.
  • SI unit is ohm.
  • Symbol for ohm is Ω.
  • Resistance depends on material, length, cross-sectional area and temperature.
  • Longer conductors generally have greater resistance.
  • Thicker conductors generally have lower resistance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Resistance → Opposition to Current

21. Ohm's Law
  • Ohm's Law states that current through a conductor is directly proportional to potential difference across it when physical conditions remain constant.
  • V ∝ I.
  • V = IR.
  • R is resistance.
  • Georg Simon Ohm formulated this law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ohm → V = IR

22. Ohmic Conductor
  • An ohmic conductor obeys Ohm's Law over the operating range.
  • Its V-I graph is a straight line through the origin when resistance is constant.
  • Metallic resistors can approximately behave as ohmic conductors under fixed temperature conditions.
23. Non-Ohmic Devices
  • Non-ohmic devices do not show a constant ratio V/I.
  • Diodes are non-ohmic.
  • Filament lamps are not perfectly ohmic because filament temperature changes.
  • Thermistors have resistance strongly dependent on temperature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Ohm's Law does not apply universally to every electrical device.

24. Factors Affecting Resistance
  • Resistance increases with length.
  • Resistance decreases with greater cross-sectional area.
  • Resistance depends on the material.
  • Resistance varies with temperature.
  • For a uniform conductor, R = ρL/A.
  • ρ is resistivity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

R = ρL/A

25. Resistivity
  • Resistivity is an intrinsic electrical property of a material.
  • Resistivity is represented by ρ.
  • SI unit is ohm metre.
  • Low resistivity means good electrical conduction.
  • Copper has low resistivity.
  • Insulators have very high resistivity.
  • Resistivity depends on temperature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Resistance depends on dimensions.

Resistivity is primarily a material property at a specified temperature.

26. Effect of Length
  • Resistance is directly proportional to length for a uniform conductor.
  • R ∝ L.
  • Doubling length approximately doubles resistance if all other conditions remain constant.
27. Effect of Area
  • Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.
  • R ∝ 1/A.
  • A thick wire has lower resistance than a thin wire of the same material and length.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Long wire → More resistance

Thick wire → Less resistance

28. Temperature and Metallic Resistance
  • Resistance of most metallic conductors increases with temperature.
  • Heating causes stronger lattice vibrations.
  • Increased lattice scattering impedes electron flow.
  • This property is used in resistance thermometers.
📌 Remember

Metal temperature ↑ → Resistance generally ↑

29. Temperature and Semiconductor Resistance
  • Semiconductor resistance generally decreases as temperature increases.
  • Heating creates more mobile charge carriers.
  • This behaviour is opposite to the usual trend in metals.
  • Thermistors may exploit strong temperature dependence.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Metals → T ↑, R ↑ generally.

Semiconductors → T ↑, R ↓ generally.

30. Superconductivity
  • Superconductivity is a state in which certain materials have zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature.
  • Superconductors also expel magnetic fields through the Meissner effect.
  • Superconductivity was discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911.
  • Mercury was the material in which superconductivity was first observed.
  • Superconductors can carry current with extremely low resistive loss.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Superconductivity → Zero Resistance → Onnes → 1911

31. Series Circuit
  • Components in series are connected along a single current path.
  • The same current flows through all components in series.
  • Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances.
  • Rs = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + ...
  • Potential differences across resistors add to the supply voltage.
  • Adding resistors in series increases total resistance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Series → Same Current

32. Parallel Circuit
  • Components in parallel are connected across the same two points.
  • Potential difference is the same across each parallel branch.
  • Current divides among branches.
  • Total current equals sum of branch currents.
  • Equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual branch resistance.
📌 Formula

1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parallel → Same Voltage

33. Series vs Parallel
  • Series circuit has one main current path.
  • Parallel circuit has multiple branches.
  • Current is same in series.
  • Voltage is same across parallel branches.
  • Adding series resistance increases total resistance.
  • Adding a parallel branch decreases equivalent resistance.
  • Domestic appliances are connected in parallel.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

House wiring → Parallel, not series.

34. Two Equal Resistors

For two equal resistors each of resistance R:

  • In series → Equivalent resistance = 2R.
  • In parallel → Equivalent resistance = R/2.
📌 Remember

Equal R:

Series → 2R

Parallel → R/2

35. Electric Power
  • Electrical power is the rate of electrical energy transfer.
  • P = VI.
  • Using Ohm's Law, P = I²R.
  • It can also be written as P = V²/R.
  • SI unit is watt.
  • Electrical appliances are commonly rated in watts or kilowatts.
📌 Must-Memorise

P = VI

P = I²R

P = V²/R

36. Electrical Energy
  • Electrical energy = Power × Time.
  • E = Pt.
  • E = VIt.
  • For resistive circuits, E = I²Rt.
  • SI unit is joule.
  • Household electricity is commonly measured in kilowatt-hours.
37. Kilowatt-Hour
  • Kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
  • 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s.
  • 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • One kWh is called one unit of electricity in household billing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 unit = 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J

38. Joule's Law of Heating
  • Electric current produces heat in a resistor.
  • H = I²Rt.
  • Heat is proportional to square of current.
  • Heat is proportional to resistance.
  • Heat is proportional to time.
  • James Prescott Joule is associated with this law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joule Heating → I²Rt

39. Applications of Heating Effect
  • Electric heater.
  • Electric iron.
  • Electric kettle.
  • Toaster.
  • Electric stove.
  • Water heater.
  • Incandescent filament lamp.
  • Fuse wire.
40. Heating Element
  • Heating elements are made of materials with suitable high resistance and high melting point.
  • Nichrome is commonly used as a heating element.
  • Nichrome is an alloy mainly containing nickel and chromium.
  • It has relatively high resistivity.
  • It resists oxidation at high temperature.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heating Element → Nichrome

41. Electric Fuse
  • A fuse protects a circuit from excessive current.
  • Fuse wire melts when current exceeds a safe value.
  • It works using the heating effect of current.
  • Fuse wire has a relatively low melting point.
  • A fuse is connected in series with the live wire.
  • A blown fuse must be replaced.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fuse → Heating Effect → Series → Live Wire

42. MCB
  • MCB stands for Miniature Circuit Breaker.
  • MCB automatically switches off a circuit during excessive current.
  • It can protect against overload and short circuit.
  • Unlike a fuse, an MCB can generally be reset after the fault is cleared.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MCB → Reusable automatic circuit protection

43. RCCB / RCD
  • RCCB stands for Residual Current Circuit Breaker.
  • RCD stands for Residual Current Device.
  • It detects imbalance between current in live and neutral conductors.
  • Such imbalance may indicate leakage of current to earth.
  • RCCB can reduce risk of serious electric shock.
  • It does not replace overcurrent protection such as an MCB.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

MCB → Overcurrent protection.

RCCB/RCD → Leakage-current protection.

44. Short Circuit
  • A short circuit occurs when current finds an unintended low-resistance path.
  • Short circuit can produce a very large current.
  • High current causes rapid heating.
  • It can damage wires and cause fire.
  • Fuse or MCB interrupts the circuit.
45. Overloading
  • Overloading occurs when excessive current is drawn from a circuit.
  • Connecting too many high-power appliances to one circuit can cause overloading.
  • Overloading causes wires to heat.
  • MCBs and fuses protect circuits from excessive current.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Short circuit and overload are both overcurrent conditions but have different causes.

46. Electric Shock
  • Electric shock occurs when electric current passes through the body.
  • Severity depends on current magnitude, path through body, duration, frequency and body resistance.
  • Wet skin lowers resistance and increases shock risk.
  • Electric shock can cause muscle contraction, burns and disturbance of heart rhythm.
  • Electrical safety devices reduce risk.
47. Earthing
  • Earthing connects exposed metal parts of appliances to the Earth through a low-resistance path.
  • It provides a safer path for leakage or fault current.
  • Earthing helps protective devices operate rapidly.
  • The earth wire normally carries no significant current during correct operation.
  • Earthing reduces risk of electric shock.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth Wire → Safety path for fault current

48. Three Wires in Domestic Wiring
  • Live wire supplies current to appliance.
  • Neutral wire provides return path.
  • Earth wire provides safety connection to exposed metal parts.
  • Appliances are connected between live and neutral.
  • Switches and fuses are placed in the live conductor.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Live → Supply

Neutral → Return

Earth → Safety

49. Colour Coding — Common Modern Standard
  • Live conductor is commonly brown.
  • Neutral conductor is commonly blue.
  • Protective earth is green-yellow.
  • Older wiring systems may use different colour conventions.
  • Always follow the applicable electrical standard rather than relying on colour alone.
50. Domestic Supply in India
  • Domestic electrical supply in India is alternating current.
  • Nominal household supply is about 230 V.
  • Standard supply frequency is 50 Hz.
  • AC frequency of 50 Hz means 50 cycles per second.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

India Domestic AC → 230 V, 50 Hz

51. Alternating Current
  • Alternating current periodically changes direction.
  • AC is abbreviated as alternating current.
  • Household electricity supply uses AC.
  • AC voltage can be conveniently stepped up or down using transformers.
  • High-voltage AC transmission reduces current for a given power and therefore reduces I²R losses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

AC → Direction changes periodically

52. Direct Current
  • Direct current flows in one direction.
  • DC is abbreviated as direct current.
  • Cells and batteries supply direct current in basic circuits.
  • Solar cells produce DC.
  • Many electronic devices operate internally on DC.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DC → One direction

53. AC vs DC
  • AC periodically reverses direction.
  • DC maintains one main direction.
  • Domestic mains supply is AC.
  • Batteries supply DC.
  • Transformers directly operate with changing current/flux and are used with AC systems.
  • Electronic adapters often convert mains AC to lower-voltage DC.
54. Frequency of AC
  • Frequency is number of complete AC cycles per second.
  • SI unit is hertz.
  • Indian mains frequency is 50 Hz.
  • 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles per second.
  • The current reverses direction twice during each cycle.
55. Electrical Transmission
  • Electrical power is transmitted at high voltage.
  • For a fixed transmitted power, higher voltage allows lower current.
  • Lower current reduces power loss in transmission lines.
  • Resistive power loss is proportional to I²R.
  • Transformers are used to change AC voltage.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

High Voltage Transmission → Current ↓ → I²R Loss ↓

56. Transformer — Basic Link
  • A transformer changes AC voltage using electromagnetic induction.
  • A step-up transformer increases voltage.
  • A step-down transformer decreases voltage.
  • Transformers do not operate on steady DC in the normal transformer principle.
  • Detailed transformer theory belongs mainly to magnetism/electromagnetic induction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Step-Up → Voltage ↑

Step-Down → Voltage ↓

57. Electric Cell
  • An electric cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
  • A cell produces potential difference between its terminals.
  • A group of cells connected together is called a battery in common usage.
  • Cells can be primary or secondary.
58. Primary Cell
  • Primary cells are generally designed for single-use discharge.
  • Their chemical reactions are not readily reversed by ordinary charging.
  • Dry cells are common primary cells.
  • Zinc-carbon cells are examples.
  • Alkaline cells are also commonly used primary cells.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Primary Cell → Usually Non-Rechargeable

59. Secondary Cell
  • Secondary cells are rechargeable.
  • Their chemical reactions can be reversed electrically within design limits.
  • Lead-acid batteries are secondary batteries.
  • Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable.
  • Nickel-metal hydride batteries are rechargeable.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Secondary Cell → Rechargeable

60. Dry Cell
  • A common zinc-carbon dry cell uses zinc as the container/anode material.
  • Manganese dioxide participates at the cathode side.
  • An electrolyte paste is used rather than a free-flowing liquid.
  • Dry cells provide DC.
  • They are commonly used in torches and small devices.
61. Lead-Acid Battery
  • Lead-acid battery is rechargeable.
  • It is widely used in automobiles.
  • Lead dioxide and lead participate as electrode materials.
  • Sulfuric acid acts as electrolyte.
  • Typical automotive batteries are assembled from multiple cells.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Car Battery → Lead-Acid

62. Lithium-Ion Battery
  • Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable.
  • They have high energy density compared with many older rechargeable battery types.
  • They are widely used in smartphones, laptops and electric vehicles.
  • Lithium ions move between electrodes during charge and discharge.
  • Battery management is important for safe operation.
63. Solar Cell
  • Solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy.
  • It works through the photovoltaic effect.
  • Silicon is a widely used semiconductor in solar cells.
  • Individual solar cells produce DC electricity.
  • Multiple cells form solar modules and panels.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solar Cell → Light → DC Electricity

64. Galvanic / Voltaic Cell
  • A galvanic cell converts spontaneous chemical energy into electrical energy.
  • Oxidation occurs at the anode.
  • Reduction occurs at the cathode.
  • Electrons flow through the external circuit from anode toward cathode.
  • Alessandro Volta developed the voltaic pile.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Volta → Voltaic Pile

65. Electrolytic Cell
  • An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.
  • Electrolysis occurs in electrolytic cells.
  • Electrical energy is converted into chemical energy.
  • Electroplating uses electrolysis.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Galvanic cell → Chemical to electrical.

Electrolytic cell → Electrical to chemical.

66. Electrolysis
  • Electrolysis is chemical decomposition or chemical change caused by electric current through an electrolyte.
  • Electrolytes conduct through movement of ions.
  • Positive ions are called cations.
  • Negative ions are called anions.
  • Cations move toward the cathode.
  • Anions move toward the anode.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cation → Cathode

Anion → Anode

67. Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
  • Michael Faraday formulated quantitative laws of electrolysis.
  • Mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to quantity of electric charge passed.
  • Q = It.
  • Electrolysis has applications in electroplating, extraction and purification of metals.
68. Electroplating
  • Electroplating deposits a thin metal coating using electric current.
  • It can improve corrosion resistance.
  • It can improve appearance.
  • Chromium plating and silver plating are examples.
  • The object to be plated is generally connected as the cathode in common electroplating arrangements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electroplating → Electrolysis

69. Ammeter
  • Ammeter measures electric current.
  • It is connected in series with the circuit element.
  • An ideal ammeter has very low resistance.
  • Current passes through the ammeter.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ammeter → Current → Series

70. Voltmeter
  • Voltmeter measures potential difference.
  • It is connected in parallel across the component.
  • An ideal voltmeter has very high resistance.
  • It draws negligible current ideally.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Voltmeter → Voltage → Parallel

71. Galvanometer
  • A galvanometer detects and measures small electric currents.
  • It can indicate direction of current.
  • A galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter using a low-resistance shunt.
  • It can be converted into a voltmeter using a high resistance in series.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Galvanometer → Small Current

72. Conversion of Galvanometer
  • Galvanometer + low resistance in parallel → Ammeter.
  • Galvanometer + high resistance in series → Voltmeter.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shunt → Ammeter

High Series Resistance → Voltmeter

73. Multimeter
  • A multimeter can measure multiple electrical quantities.
  • Common measurements include voltage, current and resistance.
  • Digital multimeters are widely used.
  • Correct range and connection must be selected for safety.
74. Electric Meter
  • Household electricity meter measures electrical energy consumption.
  • Billing is usually in kilowatt-hours.
  • One recorded unit corresponds to one kilowatt-hour.
  • Modern meters may be electronic or smart meters.
75. Resistor
  • A resistor limits current and produces voltage drops in circuits.
  • Resistance is measured in ohms.
  • Resistors convert electrical energy into heat.
  • Fixed and variable resistors are used in circuits.
76. Rheostat
  • A rheostat is a variable resistor.
  • It is used to control current in a circuit.
  • Changing effective resistance changes current.
  • Traditional rheostats use a sliding contact.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rheostat → Variable Resistance → Current Control

77. Potentiometer — Basic Fact
  • A potentiometer is a variable resistor arrangement commonly used for voltage division.
  • It has three terminals in common forms.
  • Potentiometers are used in controls such as volume adjustment and position sensing.
  • Traditional physics potentiometers can also compare potential differences accurately.
78. Electric Circuit
  • An electric circuit is a closed conducting path through which current can flow.
  • A source provides potential difference.
  • Conductors connect components.
  • A load converts electrical energy to another form.
  • A switch controls continuity of the circuit.
79. Open Circuit
  • An open circuit has a break in the conducting path.
  • Current does not flow through an ideal open circuit.
  • An open switch creates an open circuit.
80. Closed Circuit
  • A closed circuit has a complete conducting path.
  • Current can flow if a potential difference is present.
  • Closing a switch completes the circuit.
81. Short Circuit
  • Short circuit provides an unintended low-resistance path.
  • It can cause excessive current.
  • High current produces heating.
  • Protective devices interrupt the supply.
82. Switch
  • A switch opens or closes a circuit.
  • In household wiring, the switch should be connected in the live wire.
  • Switching the live conductor helps isolate the appliance from dangerous potential when off.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Switch and fuse → Live wire.

83. Domestic Parallel Connection
  • Domestic appliances are connected in parallel.
  • Each appliance receives the full supply voltage.
  • Appliances can be switched independently.
  • Failure of one appliance does not normally stop the others.
  • Different appliances can draw different currents.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Home Appliances → Parallel Circuit

84. Appliance Rating
  • Appliance power rating indicates the rate at which it uses electrical energy at its rated voltage.
  • A 1000 W heater uses more power than a 100 W lamp under rated conditions.
  • Energy consumed = Power × Time.
  • Higher-power appliances generally draw more current at the same voltage.
85. Current Drawn by Appliance
  • From P = VI:
  • I = P/V.
  • At the same voltage, a high-power appliance draws greater current.
  • This is why high-power appliances require suitable wiring and protective devices.
86. Three-Pin Plug
  • A three-pin plug provides live, neutral and earth connections.
  • The earth pin provides a safety connection.
  • In many plug designs, the earth pin is longer so earth connection is made first and broken last.
  • The earth pin is often thicker to reduce resistance and prevent incorrect insertion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Longer/Thicker Pin → Earth

87. Fuse Rating
  • Fuse rating should be slightly above the normal operating current of the appliance or circuit according to design.
  • Too low a rating causes unnecessary blowing.
  • Too high a rating may fail to provide adequate protection.
  • Fuse selection must match circuit requirements.
88. Electric Shock and Wet Hands
  • Water containing dissolved salts conducts electricity.
  • Wet skin has lower resistance than dry skin.
  • Lower resistance allows greater current for the same voltage.
  • Electrical appliances should not be handled with wet hands.
89. Birds on Power Lines
  • A bird sitting on a single wire usually has both feet at nearly the same electric potential.
  • Very little potential difference exists across its body.
  • Therefore, little current flows through it.
  • If it simultaneously touches another conductor at a very different potential, dangerous current can flow.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bird safety on one wire → Very small potential difference across body.

90. Lightning
  • Lightning is a large electrical discharge.
  • Charge separation occurs in storm clouds.
  • A large potential difference can develop.
  • Discharge may occur between clouds or between cloud and ground.
  • Lightning heats air rapidly.
  • Rapid expansion of heated air produces thunder.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lightning → Electrical Discharge

Thunder → Rapidly expanding heated air

91. Lightning Conductor
  • Benjamin Franklin's work established important understanding of lightning as electrical.
  • A lightning conductor provides a low-resistance path for lightning current to reach Earth.
  • It is installed on tall structures.
  • It protects the structure by directing current safely into the ground.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lightning Conductor → Benjamin Franklin

92. Electrostatic Discharge
  • Static charge can accumulate on clothing, vehicles and equipment.
  • A sudden discharge can produce a spark.
  • Inflammable environments require protection from static sparks.
  • Grounding helps remove excess charge safely.
93. Electrostatic Applications
  • Photocopiers use electrostatic attraction.
  • Laser printers use electrostatic charging processes.
  • Electrostatic precipitators remove particles from industrial exhaust gases.
  • Electrostatic painting helps distribute paint onto surfaces.
  • Electrostatic separation is used in some industries.
94. Electrostatic Precipitator
  • Electrostatic precipitators remove fine particles from gas streams.
  • Particles are electrically charged.
  • Charged particles are attracted to oppositely charged or grounded collecting plates.
  • They are used to reduce particulate air pollution from industrial exhaust.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electrostatic Precipitator → Removes Particulate Matter

95. Coulomb's Law
  • Coulomb's Law gives the force between point charges.
  • Force is directly proportional to product of charges.
  • Force is inversely proportional to square of distance.
  • F = kq₁q₂/r² in magnitude.
  • Charles-Augustin de Coulomb formulated the law.
  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coulomb → Electrostatic Force

96. Inverse-Square Effect
  • If distance between two point charges doubles, electrostatic force becomes one-fourth.
  • If distance triples, force becomes one-ninth.
  • This follows Coulomb's inverse-square dependence.
97. Electric Field
  • Electric field is the region where an electric charge experiences electric force.
  • Electric field strength E = F/q.
  • SI unit is N/C.
  • Direction is defined as direction of force on a positive test charge.
  • Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Electric Field → E = F/q

98. Electric Field Lines
  • Electric field lines begin on positive charges and terminate on negative charges or infinity.
  • Field lines do not cross.
  • Closer field lines indicate stronger field.
  • Tangent to a field line gives field direction.
  • Electric field lines are conceptual representations.
99. Potential and Field
  • Electric field points in the direction of decreasing electric potential for a positive test charge.
  • Equipotential surfaces have the same electric potential everywhere.
  • No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface in an electrostatic field.
100. Capacitor — Basic Fact
  • A capacitor stores electric charge and electrical potential energy.
  • It consists of two conductors separated by an insulating material called dielectric.
  • Capacitance is represented by C.
  • SI unit of capacitance is farad.
  • Capacitors are used in electronic circuits and power systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Capacitance → Farad

101. Capacitance
  • Capacitance C = Q/V.
  • Greater capacitance means more charge stored for a given voltage.
  • SI unit is farad.
  • One farad equals one coulomb per volt.
📌 Remember

1 F = 1 C/V

102. Capacitor Energy
  • Energy stored in capacitor = ½CV².
  • Capacitors store energy in the electric field.
  • Capacitors can release stored energy rapidly.
  • Camera flashes historically used capacitors to deliver short bursts of energy.
103. Dielectric
  • A dielectric is an insulating material placed between capacitor plates.
  • Dielectrics increase capacitance in common capacitor arrangements.
  • Air, paper, ceramic and plastic can serve as dielectric materials.
  • Dielectric breakdown occurs when an electric field becomes too strong.
104. Electric Energy and Heat Loss
  • Electrical transmission lines have resistance.
  • Power lost as heat = I²R.
  • Lower current greatly reduces transmission loss.
  • Increasing transmission voltage enables lower current for the same power.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Transmission Loss → I²R

105. Power Factor — Basic AC Fact
  • In AC systems, voltage and current may not always be in phase.
  • Power factor measures how effectively electrical power is converted into useful work in AC circuits.
  • Power factor ranges from 0 to 1 in basic magnitude description.
  • Industrial systems often use correction methods to improve power factor.
106. Electricity and Magnetism Link
  • Electric current produces a magnetic field.
  • This was demonstrated by Hans Christian Oersted.
  • A changing magnetic field can induce electric current.
  • Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
  • These ideas connect electricity and magnetism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Oersted → Current produces magnetic field

Faraday → Changing magnetic field induces emf

107. Oersted's Discovery
  • Hans Christian Oersted observed the magnetic effect of electric current in 1820.
  • A compass needle deflected near a current-carrying wire.
  • His discovery showed a connection between electricity and magnetism.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Oersted → 1820 → Magnetic Effect of Current

108. Faraday
  • Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
  • Changing magnetic flux can produce induced emf.
  • Faraday also formulated laws of electrolysis.
  • The SI unit of capacitance, farad, is named after him.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Faraday → Induction + Electrolysis

109. Volta
  • Alessandro Volta developed the voltaic pile.
  • The voltaic pile was an early continuous source of electric current.
  • The SI unit volt is named after Volta.
  • His work contributed to development of electrochemistry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Volta → Voltaic Pile → Volt

110. Ampère
  • André-Marie Ampère made major contributions to electrodynamics.
  • The SI unit of electric current, ampere, is named after him.
  • Ampère studied forces between current-carrying conductors.
111. Ohm
  • Georg Simon Ohm formulated Ohm's Law.
  • The SI unit of resistance, ohm, is named after him.
  • Ohm's Law is V = IR.
112. Coulomb
  • Charles-Augustin de Coulomb studied electrostatic force.
  • The SI unit of electric charge, coulomb, is named after him.
  • Coulomb's law has an inverse-square form.
113. Benjamin Franklin
  • Benjamin Franklin conducted important experiments on electricity.
  • He demonstrated the electrical nature of lightning.
  • He introduced positive and negative terminology for electric charge.
  • Lightning rods are strongly associated with his work.
114. Benjamin Franklin's Kite Experiment
  • Franklin's famous 1752 experiment involved a kite during a thunderstorm.
  • It provided evidence connecting lightning with electricity.
  • The experiment is historically important but extremely dangerous to imitate.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Franklin → Lightning is Electrical

115. Electric Current in Metals
  • Free electrons are charge carriers in metals.
  • Electrons drift opposite to conventional current direction.
  • Metallic conduction does not involve movement of positive ions through the solid lattice.
116. Electric Current in Electrolytes
  • Both positive and negative ions carry current in electrolytes.
  • Cations move toward the cathode.
  • Anions move toward the anode.
  • Chemical changes may occur at electrodes.
117. Electric Current in Gases
  • Gases normally conduct poorly.
  • Gas becomes conductive when sufficiently ionised.
  • Lightning is electrical conduction through ionised air.
  • Neon signs operate through electrical discharge in gases.
118. Electric Current in Semiconductors
  • Electrons and holes can act as charge carriers.
  • Doping modifies semiconductor conductivity.
  • n-type semiconductors have electrons as majority carriers.
  • p-type semiconductors have holes as majority carriers.
  • Semiconductor details are important in the Electronics chapter.
119. Series Combination of Cells
  • Cells connected in series can increase total emf when oriented in the same direction.
  • Positive terminal of one is connected to negative terminal of the next.
  • Series connection is useful when higher voltage is required.
120. Parallel Combination of Cells
  • Cells connected in parallel maintain approximately the same voltage as one cell when identical.
  • Parallel arrangements can provide greater current capacity and duration.
  • Cells should be properly matched for safe parallel operation.
121. EMF
  • EMF stands for electromotive force.
  • Despite its name, emf is not a force.
  • EMF is energy supplied by a source per unit charge.
  • SI unit of emf is volt.
  • A battery's emf represents the energy supplied per coulomb under ideal open-circuit conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

EMF → Measured in volts.

EMF ≠ Mechanical force.

122. Internal Resistance
  • Real cells have internal resistance.
  • When current flows, some voltage is lost inside the cell.
  • Terminal voltage can be less than emf during discharge.
  • Internal resistance causes heating and reduces efficiency.
123. Power Rating Example
  • A 1000 W appliance uses energy at 1000 joules per second.
  • If operated for one hour, it consumes 1 kWh.
  • A 2000 W appliance used for half an hour also consumes 1 kWh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Energy = Power × Time

124. Electricity Billing
  • Electricity bills are based mainly on electrical energy consumed.
  • Energy is measured in kWh.
  • Energy consumption depends on both appliance power and operating time.
  • A low-power appliance used for long hours can consume significant energy.
125. Important Electricity Formulae
  • Current → I = Q/t.
  • Potential difference → V = W/Q.
  • Ohm's Law → V = IR.
  • Resistance → R = ρL/A.
  • Series resistance → Rs = R₁ + R₂ + ...
  • Parallel resistance → 1/Rp = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...
  • Power → P = VI.
  • Power → P = I²R.
  • Power → P = V²/R.
  • Energy → E = Pt.
  • Joule heat → H = I²Rt.
  • Coulomb force → F = kq₁q₂/r².
  • Electric field → E = F/q.
  • Capacitance → C = Q/V.
  • Capacitor energy → ½CV².
126. Important SI Units
  • Charge → Coulomb.
  • Current → Ampere.
  • Potential difference → Volt.
  • Resistance → Ohm.
  • Resistivity → Ohm metre.
  • Power → Watt.
  • Electrical energy → Joule.
  • Commercial electrical energy → kWh.
  • Electric field → N/C.
  • Capacitance → Farad.
  • Frequency → Hertz.
127. Important Scientist–Unit Pairs
  • Coulomb → Electric charge.
  • Ampère → Electric current.
  • Volta → Potential difference.
  • Ohm → Resistance.
  • Watt → Power.
  • Joule → Energy.
  • Faraday → Capacitance.
  • Hertz → Frequency.
128. Important Scientist–Discovery Pairs
  • Benjamin Franklin → Electrical nature of lightning.
  • Alessandro Volta → Voltaic pile.
  • Georg Simon Ohm → Ohm's Law.
  • Charles Coulomb → Electrostatic force law.
  • André-Marie Ampère → Electrodynamics.
  • Hans Christian Oersted → Magnetic effect of current.
  • Michael Faraday → Electromagnetic induction and electrolysis.
  • James Prescott Joule → Heating effect and energy.
  • Heike Kamerlingh Onnes → Superconductivity.
129. Must-Memorise Circuit Facts
  • Ammeter → Series.
  • Voltmeter → Parallel.
  • Ammeter resistance → Very low ideally.
  • Voltmeter resistance → Very high ideally.
  • Home appliances → Parallel.
  • Fuse → Series in live wire.
  • Switch → Live wire.
  • Earth wire → Safety.
  • MCB → Overcurrent.
  • RCCB → Leakage current.
  • Series circuit → Same current.
  • Parallel circuit → Same voltage.
130. TNPSC Traps
  • Electric current is rate of flow of charge.
  • Conventional current is opposite to electron drift in metals.
  • Potential difference is measured in volts.
  • EMF is not a force.
  • Resistance and resistivity are different.
  • Resistance depends on dimensions; resistivity is a material property.
  • Metal resistance usually increases with temperature.
  • Semiconductor resistance generally decreases with temperature.
  • Ohm's Law applies only when relevant physical conditions remain constant.
  • In series, current is the same.
  • In parallel, voltage is the same.
  • Parallel equivalent resistance is less than the smallest branch resistance.
  • Household appliances are connected in parallel.
  • Watt is a unit of power.
  • kWh is a unit of energy.
  • One unit of electricity = 1 kWh.
  • Fuse works through heating effect.
  • Fuse and switch are connected in live wire.
  • Earth wire is for safety.
  • MCB and RCCB perform different protective roles.
  • Wet skin increases shock risk by reducing resistance.
  • AC reverses direction periodically.
  • Batteries supply DC.
  • Indian domestic supply is about 230 V, 50 Hz.
  • High-voltage transmission reduces I²R loss by reducing current.
  • Ammeter is connected in series.
  • Voltmeter is connected in parallel.
  • Galvanometer measures small currents.
  • Cations move to cathode.
  • Anions move to anode.
  • Galvanic cell converts chemical to electrical energy.
  • Electrolytic cell converts electrical to chemical energy.
  • Solar cell produces DC.
  • Graphite conducts electricity although it is a non-metal.
  • Lightning is an electrical discharge.
  • Thunder is caused by rapid expansion of heated air.
  • A bird on one power line is usually safe because there is little potential difference across its body.
131. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Charge → Coulomb.
  • Electron → Negative.
  • Proton → Positive.
  • Current → Q/t.
  • Ampere → C/s.
  • Voltage → W/Q.
  • 1 V → 1 J/C.
  • Resistance → Ohm.
  • Ohm → V = IR.
  • Resistivity → Ω m.
  • Series → Same current.
  • Parallel → Same voltage.
  • Power → VI.
  • Energy → Pt.
  • 1 unit → 1 kWh.
  • 1 kWh → 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
  • Heating → I²Rt.
  • Fuse → Live wire.
  • MCB → Overcurrent.
  • RCCB → Leakage.
  • Earth → Safety.
  • India → 230 V, 50 Hz AC.
  • Battery → DC.
  • Ammeter → Series.
  • Voltmeter → Parallel.
  • Galvanometer → Small current.
  • Rheostat → Variable resistance.
  • Cell → Chemical to electrical.
  • Electrolysis → Electrical to chemical.
  • Cation → Cathode.
  • Anion → Anode.
  • Solar cell → Light to DC.
  • Lightning → Discharge.
  • Oersted → Current magnetism.
  • Faraday → Induction.
  • Onnes → Superconductivity.

  • Two types of electric charge? → Positive and negative.
  • Like charges? → Repel.
  • Unlike charges? → Attract.
  • SI unit of charge? → Coulomb.
  • Charge of electron? → −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Charge of proton? → +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

  • Is electric charge conserved? → Yes.
  • Q = ne represents? → Quantisation of charge.
  • Static electricity means? → Accumulated electric charge.
  • Charging without contact? → Induction.
  • Charging by physical contact? → Conduction.
  • Common electrical conductor? → Copper.
  • Non-metal that conducts electricity? → Graphite.
  • Common semiconductor? → Silicon.
  • Electric current means? → Rate of flow of charge.
  • Current formula? → I = Q/t.
  • SI unit of current? → Ampere.
  • 1 ampere equals? → 1 C/s.
  • Direction of conventional current compared with electron flow in metal? → Opposite.
  • Potential difference formula? → V = W/Q.
  • SI unit of potential difference? → Volt.
  • 1 volt equals? → 1 J/C.
  • Opposition to current? → Resistance.
  • SI unit of resistance? → Ohm.
  • Ohm's Law? → V = IR.
  • Scientist associated with Ohm's Law? → Georg Simon Ohm.
  • Resistance formula using resistivity? → R = ρL/A.
  • Resistance increases with? → Length.
  • Resistance decreases with? → Cross-sectional area.
  • SI unit of resistivity? → Ohm metre.
  • Temperature rise effect on metallic resistance? → Generally increases.
  • Temperature rise effect on semiconductor resistance? → Generally decreases.
  • Zero electrical resistance below critical temperature? → Superconductivity.
  • Superconductivity discovered by? → Heike Kamerlingh Onnes.
  • Year of superconductivity discovery? → 1911.
  • First material observed superconducting? → Mercury.
  • In series circuit, same quantity through all components? → Current.
  • Series equivalent resistance? → Sum of resistances.
  • In parallel circuit, same quantity across branches? → Voltage.
  • Parallel equivalent resistance compared with smallest branch? → Smaller.
  • Domestic appliances connected in? → Parallel.

  • Other power formulas? → I²R and V²/R.
  • SI unit of power? → Watt.
  • Electrical energy formula? → E = Pt.
  • Commercial unit of electrical energy? → kWh.
  • One electricity unit? → 1 kWh.
  • 1 kWh equals? → 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

  • Heating element commonly made of? → Nichrome.
  • Fuse works on? → Heating effect of electric current.
  • Fuse connected in? → Series.
  • Fuse placed in which wire? → Live wire.
  • MCB stands for? → Miniature Circuit Breaker.
  • MCB protects against? → Excess current due to overload/short circuit.
  • RCCB stands for? → Residual Current Circuit Breaker.
  • RCCB mainly detects? → Leakage current to earth.
  • Purpose of earthing? → Provide low-resistance fault-current path and reduce shock risk.
  • Three domestic wires? → Live, neutral and earth.
  • Switch connected in? → Live wire.
  • Nominal Indian household voltage? → About 230 V.
  • Indian mains frequency? → 50 Hz.
  • AC means? → Alternating Current.
  • DC means? → Direct Current.
  • Battery supplies? → DC.
  • Domestic mains supplies? → AC.
  • Why transmit electricity at high voltage? → To reduce current and I²R losses.
  • Step-up transformer does? → Increases voltage.
  • Step-down transformer does? → Decreases voltage.
  • Cell converts? → Chemical energy to electrical energy.
  • Primary cell? → Generally non-rechargeable.
  • Secondary cell? → Rechargeable.
  • Common automobile battery? → Lead-acid battery.
  • Electrolyte in lead-acid battery? → Sulfuric acid.
  • Common rechargeable phone battery? → Lithium-ion.
  • Solar cell converts? → Light energy to electrical energy.
  • Solar cell output is primarily? → DC.
  • Galvanic cell converts? → Chemical to electrical energy.
  • Electrolytic cell converts? → Electrical to chemical energy.
  • Electrolysis means? → Chemical change caused by electric current through electrolyte.
  • Positive ion? → Cation.
  • Negative ion? → Anion.
  • Cation moves to? → Cathode.
  • Anion moves to? → Anode.
  • Electroplating is based on? → Electrolysis.

  • Ammeter connected in? → Series.
  • Ideal ammeter resistance? → Very low.
  • Voltmeter measures? → Potential difference.

  • Instrument measuring voltage, current and resistance? → Multimeter.
  • Household electricity meter measures? → Electrical energy in kWh.
  • Variable resistor? → Rheostat.
  • Closed conducting path? → Electric circuit.
  • Broken conducting path? → Open circuit.
  • Unintended low-resistance path? → Short circuit.
  • Why are wet hands dangerous near electricity? → Wet skin has lower resistance.
  • Why can a bird sit on a single power line? → Very little potential difference across its body.

  • Thunder is caused by? → Rapid expansion of air heated by lightning.
  • Lightning conductor associated with? → Benjamin Franklin.
  • Electrostatic precipitator removes? → Particulate matter from exhaust gases.
  • Coulomb's Law describes? → Force between electric charges.
  • Coulomb force relation with distance? → Inversely proportional to r².

  • SI unit of electric field? → N/C.
  • Electric field direction is defined using? → Positive test charge.
  • Electric field lines from positive charge point? → Outward.
